title: Jalapeño Hot Chip, Cool Power Bill: OpenAI Turns Up the Heat on AI Inference - Semiwiki
gist: OpenAI's custom inference ASIC 'Jalapeño' (up to 13.4 PFLOPS MXFP4, 216GiB HBM4, 700W package, scaling to a 2,048-chip/27-exaflop system) uses a spatial core-plus-local-HBM architecture and power-gating to optimize tokens-per-joule and time-between-tokens rather than peak FLOPS, and per OpenAI's own InferenceX benchmark disclosure beats selected NVIDIA GB200/GB300 configurations by 1.5-4.1x on several efficiency metrics — with OpenAI going from RTL to tape-out in nine months using AI-generated kernels.

themes.theme: Jalapeño's design philosophy: latency/efficiency over peak FLOPS

insights.claim: OpenAI designed Jalapeño around the thesis that useful inference performance cannot be reduced to peak floating-point operations or memory bandwidth; instead OpenAI evaluates the chip on end-to-end latency, time between tokens, and tokens per joule across the full latency-throughput trade-off.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in how the leading AI lab benchmarks inference silicon — away from raw FLOPS/bandwidth specs (NVIDIA's traditional marketing metrics) toward system-level, request-completion efficiency metrics; investors comparing AI accelerators should weight tokens-per-joule and time-between-tokens over peak TFLOPS claims.
insights.quote: Its central idea is that useful performance cannot be reduced to peak floating-point operations or memory bandwidth. What matters is how quickly and efficiently the complete request finishes.
insights.locator: OpenAI's Jalapeño is a custom accelerator designed specifically for AI inference

insights.claim: Although Jalapeño's aggregate HBM bandwidth theoretically permits thousands of full-model weight reads per second, OpenAI states practical token rates remain far lower because data movement, synchronization, communication, and late-arriving operands leave compute units waiting.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A vendor-stated causal explanation for why headline bandwidth/FLOPS specs overstate real-world inference throughput — relevant for discounting peak-spec marketing across the whole AI-accelerator category, not just Jalapeño.
insights.quote: Although aggregate HBM bandwidth theoretically permits thousands of full-model weight reads per second, practical token rates remain far lower because data movement, synchronization, communication, and late-arriving operands leave compute units waiting.
insights.locator: The ASIC combines substantial compute and memory capacity

insights.claim: OpenAI states that unused compute/memory/networking blocks inside a Jalapeño package can be power-gated, on the reasoning that 'dark' silicon inside one package costs less than idle accelerators that keep consuming baseline HBM, networking, cooling, and rack resources.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A concrete power-efficiency design principle (power-gate idle silicon rather than let whole idle accelerators draw baseline power) directly tied to reducing datacenter opex — relevant to evaluating inference-chip TCO claims across vendors.
insights.quote: OpenAI’s guiding observation is that “dark” silicon inside one package costs less than idle accelerators that continue consuming baseline HBM, networking, cooling, and rack resources.
insights.locator: This organization reflects the changing demands within a single inference request

insights.claim: The Jalapeño ASIC delivers up to 13.4 petaflops of MXFP4 matrix compute, 216 GiB of HBM4 memory, and 15.4 TB/s of memory bandwidth within a 700-watt package.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Concrete per-chip spec benchmark for comparing Jalapeño against NVIDIA GB200/GB300 and other custom inference ASICs (e.g. Google TPU, Amazon Trainium/Inferentia, Broadcom-designed chips) on a compute/memory/power-per-package basis.
insights.quote: up to 13.4 petaflops of MXFP4 matrix compute, 216 GiB of HBM4, and 15.4 TB/s of memory bandwidth within a 700-watt package
insights.locator: The ASIC combines substantial compute and memory capacity

insights.claim: A complete 2,048-chip Jalapeño system reaches 27 exaflops of MXFP4 compute, 432 TiB of aggregate memory, and 32 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth, with 128 chips forming a local domain and up to 2,048 chips connected via a two-level Clos network with deliberately tapered bandwidth (tensor parallelism gets higher bandwidth, expert parallelism needs less).
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: System-scale spec (27 exaflops MXFP4 at 2,048 chips) is the figure to benchmark against rival hyperscaler in-house inference-cluster designs (Google TPU pods, Amazon Trainium clusters, Microsoft Maia) when assessing OpenAI's compute self-sufficiency roadmap.
insights.quote: A complete 2,048-chip system reaches 27 exaflops of MXFP4 compute, 432 TiB of memory, and 32 PB/s of aggregate bandwidth.
insights.locator: At system scale, 128 chips form a local domain

insights.claim: Jalapeño uses a spatial architecture where each core slice is paired with its own HBM slice for fast local memory access; specialized collective networks handle common cross-core communication patterns while a more flexible network-on-chip handles general traffic, and software explicitly places tensors and computes locally to avoid costly global synchronization fences.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Describes the core architectural mechanism (local core+HBM pairing, explicit tensor placement, distributed control avoiding global fences) behind Jalapeño's claimed efficiency gains — a technical benchmark for evaluating competing inference-chip architectures' approaches to the same synchronization-overhead problem.
insights.locator: Jalapeño addresses these bottlenecks through a spatial architecture

insights.claim: Jalapeño's architecture keeps state local across the differing demands of an inference request's phases (compute-bound attention-heavy prefill, latency-sensitive low-batch speculative drafting, and memory-bandwidth-intensive mixture-of-experts verification/decoding with bursty communication) rather than assigning each phase to separate accelerators and repeatedly transferring the key-value cache.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A specific technical rationale for unified (versus disaggregated-by-phase) inference chip design; relevant when comparing Jalapeño's approach against disaggregated prefill/decode inference-serving architectures used elsewhere in the industry.
insights.locator: Prefill is attention-heavy and largely compute-bound

themes.theme: Benchmark claims against NVIDIA and development timeline

insights.claim: On the public InferenceX benchmark, OpenAI reports Jalapeño sits on the performance-per-watt Pareto frontier for GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek R1 670B, and Kimi K2.5 1T, and against selected NVIDIA GB200 or GB300 configurations reports 1.5-1.9x greater peak throughput per kilowatt, 1.7-3.6x lower end-to-end latency, and 2.1-4.1x better token interactivity, using 8,000-token inputs, 1,000-token outputs, four-bit weights, package-TDP normalization, and vendor-optimized software.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Directly quantifies OpenAI's claimed efficiency edge over NVIDIA's current flagship inference GPUs (GB200/GB300) — material for anyone modeling NVIDIA's competitive moat against hyperscaler/lab custom silicon, though this is OpenAI's own vendor-selected benchmark disclosure and should be treated as a self-reported claim, not independently verified.
insights.quote: Against the selected GB200 or GB300 configurations, the deck reports 1.5–1.9 times greater peak throughput per kilowatt, 1.7–3.6 times lower end-to-end latency, and 2.1–4.1 times better token interactivity.

insights.claim: OpenAI reports that at the previous system's time-between-token point, Jalapeño's efficiency advantage over the prior (GB200/GB300-based) system ranges from 8.6x to 104.3x, and notes Jalapeño uses single-token prediction while some baselines it is compared against use multi-token prediction, making the disclosed methodology essential to interpreting the results.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The very wide 8.6x-104.3x claimed range, combined with OpenAI's own caveat about mismatched single- vs multi-token-prediction baselines, is a flag for investors to treat this specific figure skeptically pending third-party replication rather than take it as an apples-to-apples GPU comparison.
insights.quote: Importantly, Jalapeño uses single-token prediction while some baselines use multi-token prediction, making the disclosed methodology essential when interpreting the results.
insights.locator: At the previous system's time-between-token point

insights.claim: OpenAI took Jalapeño from initial RTL to tape-out in nine months, using AI to optimize hardware blocks and to generate kernels that reportedly exceeded expert-written implementations.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A nine-month RTL-to-tape-out cycle, if accurate, is materially faster than typical custom-silicon development timelines and signals AI-assisted chip design (AI-generated kernels beating expert-written code) is now a credible accelerant for custom AI-accelerator programs — relevant to EDA vendors and other labs/hyperscalers considering in-house silicon.
insights.quote: OpenAI moved from initial RTL to tape-out in nine months, used AI to optimize hardware blocks, and generated kernels that reportedly exceeded expert-written implementations.
insights.locator: Jalapeño also demonstrates the value of hardware-software-AI co-design

insights.claim: The article's bottom-line framing is that inference is becoming the dominant operational cost of AI, and that agentic applications invoking models repeatedly before completing one user task make requests-per-second-per-watt improvements translate directly into lower energy consumption, greater datacenter capacity, and faster interactive systems — with the broader strategic implication that model developers can now shape silicon around real workloads, shortening the loop between algorithms, compilers, architecture, and deployment.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Frames custom inference silicon as a strategic cost-control lever as inference (versus training) becomes AI's dominant compute cost driver, especially under agentic workloads that multiply model calls per task — a thesis relevant to capex allocation decisions across AI labs and cloud providers moving toward in-house chips.
insights.quote: Bottom line: Inference is becoming the dominant operational cost of AI, while agentic applications may invoke models repeatedly before completing one user task.
